fields.title: Circadian Regulation of Protein Cargo in Exosomes
fields.description: The circadian clock controls many aspects of physiology, but it remains undescribed whether extracellular vesicles (including exosomes) involved in cell-cell communications between tissues are regulated in a circadian pattern. We demonstrate a 24 h rhythmic abundance of individual proteins in exosomes using liquid chromatography-mass spectrometry in circadian-synchronised tendon fibroblasts. Further, the release of exosomes enriched in RNA-binding proteins was temporally separated from those enriched in cytoskeletal and matrix proteins, which peaked during the end of the light phase. Finally, we targeted the protein sorting mechanism in the exosome biogenesis pathway and established (by knockdown of circadian-regulated flotillin-1) that matrix metalloproteinase 14 abundance in tendon fibroblast exosomes is under flotillin-1 regulation. In conclusion, we have identified proteomic time signatures for exosomes released by tendon fibroblasts which supports the view that the circadian clock regulates protein cargo in exosomes involved in cell-cell crosstalk.
fields.sample_protocol: Time series exosome protein isolation In our experimental set up samples were isolated independently for each 24 h time series, i.e. samples for 4, 8, 12, 16, 20 and 24 h after synchronisation were isolated from one experiment, samples for 28, 32, 36, 40, 44 and 48 h after synchronisation were isolated from another experiment. For each set of time series samples (4-24 h (n=3), 28-48 h (n=3), and control 4- 24 h (n=3)), isolates from two independent experiments were pooled together for sufficient material for analysis. Exosomes pellets resulting from ultracentrifugation of the 34 and 40% sucrose fractions from each experiment were resuspended and lysed with 6 M guanidine hydrochloride, 10 mM Tris (2-carboxyethyl) phosphine hydrochloride, 40 mM 2-chloroacetamide, 100 mM Tris pH 8.5 for mass spectrometry (MS) analysis. Protein concentrations were determined by Quick Start Bradford Protein Assay (Bio-Rad) according to manufacturer’s instructions.  Tryptic digestion of exosome proteins and LC-MS Exosome proteins were digested for LC-MS as described previously (ref fibroblast paper). Samples for the first 24 h, second 24 h and control time series were processed in three batches. For each sample, 500 ng peptides were loaded onto a 2-cm C18 trap column (Thermo Fisher Scientific), connected in-line to a 50-cm C18 reverse-phase analytical column (Easy-Spray LC column, Thermo Fisher Scientific) using 0.1% formic acid in water at 750 bar, using the Easy-nLC 1200 high-performance liquid chromatography system (Thermo Fisher Scientific), and the column oven operating at 45oC. Peptides were eluted over a 140-minute gradient ranging from 6% to 60% of 80% acetonitrile, 0.1% formic acid at 250 nl/min, and the Orbitrap Fusion instrument (Thermo Fisher Scientific) was run in a data-dependent-MS/MS (DD-MS2) top speed method. Full MS spectra were collected at a resolution of 120 000, with an AGC target of 4x105 or maximum injection time of 50 ms and a scan range of 400–1500 m/z. The MS2 spectra were obtained in the ion trap operating at rapid speed, with an AGC target value of 1x104 or maximum injection time of 35 ms, a normalised higher-energy collisional dissociation (HCD) collision energy of 30 and an intensity threshold of 1.7e4. Dynamic exclusion was set to 60 s, and ions with a charge state <2, >7 or unknown were excluded. MS performance was verified for consistency by running complex cell lysate quality control standards, and chromatography was monitored to check for reproducibility.
